title: Judges receive cautious green light for AI use in new position statement
source_used: Legal Futures (the Law Society Gazette page could not be opened)
key_facts: Sir Colin Birss, the judiciary's lead judge for AI and president of the Business and Property Division, becomes Master of the Rolls next month; Legal Futures says he issued a position statement on the judicial use of AI last week.
The statement complements guidance for judicial office holders first published in December 2023 and last updated a year ago.

Sir Colin said AI offers "potentially transformative implications for justice" and the judiciary's approach will be "cautious but positive"; the technology would support but not replace judicial decision-making and be subject to strict safeguards and robust testing.
The statement says every AI output used in judicial work must be reviewed, verified and approved by the responsible judicial office holder, who remains fully accountable.

Pilots examined summarisation, transcription, redaction, writing in accessible language, administrative and leadership tasks, chronology-building and document analysis, and tested reliability, the degree of human checking needed and the handling of sensitive material.
Only approved AI tools may be used; their features must include UK data residency, enterprise data protection and disabled web access.
quote_evidence: Every AI output used in judicial work must be reviewed, verified and approved by the responsible judicial office holder.
The judiciary is taking a cautious but positive approach to AI adoption, supported by pilots, evaluation, training, governance and transparency, to maintain public confidence and uphold open justice.
The statement said only approved AI tools may be used.
why_it_matters_hint: Judges are cleared to use approved AI tools for tasks such as summarising and transcription, but each judge stays fully accountable for every output.
event_date: Position statement issued 'last week' per Legal Futures (12 Oct 2026); exact date not stated.
